processing: Presumably made as other mountain-named sheng is: wok-fixed, rolled and sun-dried, then sold loose or pressed. Nothing specific to this tea is documented.
harvest_season: Spring is usually the prized picking for Yunnan mountain teas; no local detail is documented.
appearance_dry: Typical of Yunnan sheng: long dark green leaf with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow when young, as is typical of sheng.
appearance_wet: As with other large-leaf sheng, thick olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: No reliable local taste description exists. Expect what is typical of young large-leaf sheng: fresh and woody with some bitterness.

brewing.notes: Usual young sheng approach: quick rinse and short early steeps, then adjust to what the leaf does.

vintage_note: As with other mountain-named sheng, expect it sold by spring harvest year, mostly young maocha. A Chinese spring price list of 100 named Yunnan mountains gave 800 to 1,200 yuan per kilo for it, well below the top of that list and above its neighbouring entries.
description:
Guoditang is a place name used for Yunnan sheng, listed among a hundred named tea mountains in a Chinese spring price list. Beyond that, very little is written about it, and even its exact location needs checking with whoever sells it.

Nothing specific is recorded about its making, so assume the ordinary method for mountain sheng.

The same goes for taste. Treat it as an unknown young sheng, brew short, and form your own view.

If you come across it, ask which village and county it comes from and what year it was picked. Without those, the name is hard to verify.
history: Little is documented about this tea. Its clearest appearance is a published list of spring prices for 100 well-known Yunnan mountains, where it is entry 61. Its history, makers and origin in more detail are not established.
